drug_class: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor — a type of targeted cancer therapy
purpose: Ibrutinib is used to treat certain types of blood cancers, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma, and a few other blood or lymph node cancers. It may also be used for a condition called chronic graft-versus-host disease. Your doctor chose this medicine because it targets the specific type of cancer cells causing your illness.
how_it_works: Think of cancer cells as having an 'on switch' that tells them to keep growing and multiplying out of control. Ibrutinib works by blocking a protein called BTK, which is like turning off that switch. Without this signal, the cancer cells stop growing and eventually die off, while your healthy cells are much less affected.
common_side_effects: Diarrhea, feeling tired or weak, nausea, muscle or joint aches, rash, swelling in your hands or feet, bruising more easily than usual, and upper respiratory infections like a stuffy or runny nose. Some people also notice a drop in blood cell counts.
warnings: This medicine can increase your risk of serious bleeding, so let your doctor know if you take blood thinners or aspirin. It can also raise your risk of infections, heart rhythm problems (like atrial fibrillation), and high blood pressure. Avoid grapefruit and Seville oranges while taking ibrutinib, as they can increase the drug level in your blood. Tell your doctor about all your other medications, because many drugs can interact with ibrutinib. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on which condition is being treated, but it is commonly taken once a day by mouth, with or without food. Capsules or tablets should be swallowed whole — do not open, break, or chew them. Try to take it at the same time every day, and if you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and continue your normal schedule.
